chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In this video, we are going to cover containers in Python,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: i.e. data structures that can contain multiple types of data.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: More specifically, I am talking about lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Let's talk about those.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In Python, it is fairly trivial to store a single variable.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: All you need is a variable name, and then you assign it one value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Let's say the string bob in this case, could also be a number, it really doesn't matter.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But what if you want to store multiple users inside of a single variable?

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: For that, Python has the data types I just talked about, lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: The first kind of container I want to talk about is a tuple.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This one is created with normal parentheses.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: We need one to open it and one to close it.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Inside of it, you can add whatever kind of data you want.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This could for example be a string, it could be an integer,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: or it could be another tuple, which could even contain another tuple itself.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And as far as a tuple is concerned, a tuple inside of it is just another value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Meaning you could have a tuple inside of a tuple inside of another tuple,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: all with their own individual values, and this would be totally fine.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Sometimes this is necessary, but usually not something you want to do,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: because it would be quite messy to work with.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But anyway, this is a tuple.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Next up, we have a list.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Which looks very similar compared to a tuple,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: the only major difference, at least for now,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: is that we are using square brackets instead of round ones.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Other than that, we are still adding individual values,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: separated by a comma.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And that's all you need.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: So to summarize, a tuple or a list are created with parentheses or square brackets,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and then you have comma separated values.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Now you might be wondering, what's the difference between the two?

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And well, the key difference is, that a tuple cannot be changed.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: The fancy word for that is, it's immutable.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Meaning once you have a tuple, you cannot change it anymore.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Whereas for a list, you can easily add or remove values,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: or make changes to basically whatever you want.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And that's pretty much it.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In practice, when you are using them, they are more or less interchangeable.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: For most occasions, you can use either one of the two, it's totally fine.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: We will explore that in just a second in a bit more detail.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But anyway, first of all, we have to talk about this set.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: That one is defined by curly brackets.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But other than that, we still have comma separated values.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And these could be any kind of value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: So integers, strings or any other data type would be perfectly fine.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Now what is making a set unique, is that every single entry is unique on its own.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Meaning any duplicate value inside of a set will be removed.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: There are a few more extra things for a set, but those are a bit more advanced,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: so I'm not going to worry about them too much.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Finally, we have a dictionary.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And this one has quite a different data structure.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: We still have curly brackets, like we have for a set.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Which might be a bit confusing.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But the major difference for a dictionary is that we don't have individual values anymore.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Instead, we have what is called a key-value pair.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Where in this case, for example, the name is the key, and bob is the value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: After that, we have a comma separation, bit hard to see.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Then we have another key, along with another value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And this can continue forever.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Both the key and the value could be any kind of data type.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: At least within some minor limitations.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Because of that, it's quite easy to separate a dictionary and a set,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: because ultimately they are quite different.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: They just share the curly brackets, but that's about it.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And dictionaries are what you want to use if you want to have really organized data.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: It can be incredibly powerful, but also sometimes it can be a bit too much work to deal with.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But anyway, let's work with all of them in practice.

chunks.text: Once again, I am in VS Code, and I want to create a new file.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Let's call this one containers.py.

chunks.text: And let's start with some basic data types.

chunks.text: I want to, for example, create e to help.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: To create this one, I need basic parentheses.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And in there, I can add any kind of value.

chunks.text: And that's the basics of it.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If I now print e tuple and run the code, we can see that we have a list of items.

chunks.text: Next up, I want to create e list.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This one works in basically the same way.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: The only difference is now that we need square brackets,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: where we can add the exact same values.

chunks.title: Containers

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If I print this one, print e list and run the code,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: we can see we have the output of a list,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: which is looking very similar compared to a tuple.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: On top of that, you can also use a couple of functions along with both lists and tuples.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: For example, what you could be doing is place either a list or tuple

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: inside of the len function, then run the code again,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and we get the number of items inside of the list.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In this case, 4.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This would work with a list and a tuple perfectly fine.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: I can run the code again and we once again get 4.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Perfect.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: What you can also do with a list is append another value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This happens with the append method.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This method wants to have a single argument,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: which could be whatever value you want to append.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Let's say I want to add the string of another word.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: After we have that, we can print e list once more, run the code,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and now we get the list with another word at the end.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And with that, we can also talk about the difference between a tuple and a list.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Because a list can be changed, but a tuple cannot be changed.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Meaning I couldn't append a value to a tuple.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If I try that, a tuple and try to append a value,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and let's print a tuple afterwards, although it's not going to work,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: we are getting an error.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: That a tuple object has no attribute append.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Python is basically saying that there is no way to append a value to a tuple.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And if you want to make sure that your code is always working,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: just use a list, this one is much easier to work with.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And in most cases you can use either a list or a tuple,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and your code would work perfectly fine.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But anyway, for now, let's simply add a comment where we have the containers…

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Let's call it container, setup actually.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Next up, we can work with a set.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: A set is defined with curly brackets.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And in there, once again, you can add whatever value you want.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If I print the result, a set, we get, once again, some kind of data structure.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Now what is really useful about a set, is that every single value has to be unique.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Meaning if I add the for twice, and run all of this again, we are getting the same result.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In some specific circumstances, this can be incredibly useful.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: As a matter of fact, sets for data analysis are really useful.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: There are quite a few methods where you can compare two sets,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and see which values they have in common, or which are different,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: which can be an incredibly powerful feature in specific circumstances.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Although in practice, how sets are being used, is if you have a list or a tuple,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and you want to remove any duplicate value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: What you could be doing, is, let's say for the list, I have the value 2 twice.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And I want to get rid of it.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But I don't know at the moment, which value is a duplicate.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Just imagine that this list has a few thousand entries,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and I don't want to manually look through it, and see which value is a duplicate.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: To make that automatic, you can use the set function.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This one takes any kind of container, and turns it into a set.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Let me actually print it twice.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: I want to print once the original elist.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And then I want to print it again, after turning it into a set.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: So set, and then elist.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If I now run the code again,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: we are getting first of all the list,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: with all the original values that we have gotten up here.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But once we're turning it into a set,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: we are getting rid of the 2 at the end,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and only keep the original values.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And if you want to retain the list,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: you can wrap the result of the set,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: once again into another function, which is called list.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Which turns any kind of container into a list.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: So now if I run it again,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: we have elist once again, but without any duplicate value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In practice, when you see a set, this is what they are mostly used for.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: So list, set, and then elist inside of it, is a fairly common operation.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Next up, we can work with eDictionary.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This one is also defined by curly brackets.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Except now, we don't have individual values,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: instead we have key-value pairs.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Both the key and the value could be any kind of data type.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: For example, I could have a string, that I can call key,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and then another string, which should be the value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: I could also have a key called 1,2,3,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and then the value could be a list with 1,2, and 3.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Both are totally fine,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: let me print the result, eDictionary.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And what we get is the key-value pairs of the dictionary.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And once again, a dictionary can also be used with the len function for example,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and there are a couple of specific methods that can make this one incredibly useful.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But the main reason why you would use a dictionary,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: is because you can address every single value quite easily.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Once again, imagine that you don't have two key-value pairs,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: but more something like 10.000.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: With a tuple or a list, you could only access value by the index number.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: So you could get the first, the second or the third item,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: but for a dictionary, you could always access a specific name.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Which is much easier to remember,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and also much easier to work with in, well once again, specific circumstances.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But anyway, these are the four major container types in Python,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: that you have to be aware of.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Although next up, we will have to work with them a bit more.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And the part that I want to work on, is how to get values from a container.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: For that, we have to cover just a little bit of theory.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: The process we have to learn about is called indexing.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Basically how it works.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Imagine we have a list or a tuple with five entries.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Internally for Python, every single item is going to get an index.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This one starts at 0, and then increases by 1 for every single item.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: The first item has the index 0, the second item the index 1,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: the third item the index 2, and so on.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This behavior you can use by simply adding another set of square brackets after the container,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and then you are getting one specific item returned.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In this case, index 1 would give us Bob.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: So this would be returned.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This process can also become more powerful, and then it's called slicing.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Once again, we have a list, could also be a tuple,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and we also have the indexes.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Imagine now you want to get multiple items.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Let's say you want to get from Bob to Anna.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: For that, you could add a square bracket with up to three values.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: The first item would be the start value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In our case, index 1 would once again be Bob.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: The second number, so the 4, would be the end value.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And really important, which can be very confusing,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: this 4 is only the value that we go up to.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: It is not included in our selection.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Meaning, when you specify 4, you might think we are getting to John,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: but we are only moving up to this index, we are not including it.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This is a source of many errors, and especially in the beginning, can be very confusing.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This is very much something you want to practice on your own.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But anyway, the third value, the 2 in my case, is the step size.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: By default, this is 1.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: We always go up by one number.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: However, if you specify a 2 here, you are going from a 1,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: two steps to the next item, which would be index number 3.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And well, that's the basics of how to get data from a container.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Let's practice this one.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And just to be a bit more consistent with the slides,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: let me create another variable, user list,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: which is going to be the list I just had in the slides,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: where we have 5 names.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In your case, you could simply add the numbers in here.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: The logic is going to be the same.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Also, I am going to comment out all the stuff we have done before,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: so it doesn't get too confusing.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Now, let me simply print the user list on its own.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If I now run the code, we are getting the items inside of the list.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: That's a good start.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But now, I want to add square brackets after this list,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: where I can specify a number.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: This number could, for example, be 0.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And if I run it again, we now get Lisa,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: which is item number 1 inside of the list.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Since Python starts counting from 0,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: this would be the very first item, or item with the index 0.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If you change this 0 to a 1, we should get Bob.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And we do.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If we add a 2, then we are getting Alex, and so on.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: I hope the system makes sense.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: What you could also do is add a negative number.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Let's say negative 1.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In that case, we would get to John.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: The way this is working is that the first item is always index 0,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and then minus 1 would be the last item,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: minus 2 would be one further to the left, and then so on.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: We are just going in the opposite direction.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: That's all that's happening in here.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And that is indexing.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: To make this system more powerful, you could add two values in there.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: For example, I want to go from 0 to index, let's say 3.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And what we are going to get now.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If I run the code, we are getting Lisa, Bob and Alex.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Lisa has index 0, Bob 1, Alex 2 and Anna 3.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And we specified that we want to go from 0, so this index, up to index 3.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But we did not want to include that index.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And as a consequence, we get Lisa, Bob and Alex.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And if you want to expand that system, you can add another double colon,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and then specify the step size.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: For example, if you add a 2 in here, we are starting with Lisa,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and then jumping two steps and going straight to Alex.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: I guess once again, Lisa has index 0, Bob is 1 and Alex is 2.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And we told Python that we want to start on index 0, meaning on Lisa,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: then we want to go up to the third index, meaning up to Anna, but not include it.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And we only want to have every second item.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: So we start with 0, then we skip 1 and go straight to 2, which would be Alex.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Those are the values we get at the end.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Slicing and indexing is an incredibly powerful system,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: and something you definitely want to practice.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Also I should mention, you can use slicing and indexing both with a list and with a tuple.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If I replace the square brackets, and turn this list into a tuple,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: by using basic parentheses.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: If I now run the code again, we are getting the same outcome,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: the only difference now is we are getting a tuple returned instead of a list.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: But that's about it.

chunks.text: Now if you wanted to get the values from a dictionary,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: let me copy, or rather uncomment the dictionary.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: You obviously couldn't use indexing on this one, because we don't really have indexing.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Instead we have key value pairs.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: To work with that, instead of using the index,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: we simply have to add, let me print a dictionary,

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: you simply have to add the key that you want to work with.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: In fact VS Code is giving me a suggestion.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: It wants to have a key.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: And in this dictionary we have key and 123.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: So if I put in 123, we should be getting this key value pair.

chunks.title: Containers
chunks.text: Or more specifically, if you are doing that,

chunks.title: Containers
